claims.text: The target components are boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment and currently lack an additional corrosion-mitigation layer.
A thin, uniform silicide coating will act as a diffusion barrier against molten-aluminum attack on boride-based components.
The silicide coating will significantly reduce corrosion relative to uncoated boride-based components.
Silicide coatings can be applied by pack cementation.
Pack cementation will form a controlled, layered silicide film on the boride component surface.
Approximately 660 °C represents a typical molten-aluminum hot-dip-plating exposure temperature.
The coating will remain protective during standard thermal cycling if its adherence and integrity are maintained.
The intervention will produce a uniform two-layer silicide film.
Minor cracks in the silicide film can partially self-heal through local oxidation products that seal the defects.
Oxidation-assisted crack sealing will preserve the coating's barrier properties.
The silicide coating reduces molten-aluminum corrosion by limiting interdiffusion between aluminum and the boride substrate.
Self-healing behavior of this kind has been observed in silicide-coated high-entropy alloys.
The coating may reduce corrosive attack by roughly one order of magnitude relative to an uncoated baseline.
Uncoated boride-based components are more susceptible to molten-aluminum-induced corrosion than silicide-coated components.
Excessive thermal-expansion mismatch or severe mechanical stress can cause coating failure.
Coating adhesion and integrity under repeated thermal cycling bound the intervention's effectiveness.
The proposed controlled experiment compares coated and uncoated boride-based components under identical molten-aluminum exposure and thermal-cycling conditions.
Failure to obtain statistically significantly lower weight loss and penetration depth in the coated group would falsify the hypothesis.
